title: Rumores de ruptura criptográfica, fuga de capital en Taiwán y choque de escuelas con Google
script:
Bienvenidos a Radio IA, hoy es 28 de noviembre de 2026. Hoy vamos a hablar de secretos matemáticos que podrían tambalear la seguridad global, de dinero que huye de Taiwán y de una batalla entre escuelas y gigantes tecnológicos. Pero antes, abrimos con una noticia que toca la confianza en los sistemas financieros.

Según The Guardian, varios laboratorios de inteligencia artificial podrían estar guardando revelaciones explosivas capaces de alterar los cimientos de la seguridad de bancos y gobiernos en tan solo unos meses. Scott Aaronson, científico teórico de la computación, habla de rumores bien documentados de que modelos potentes de IA han abierto camino en problemas matemáticos con décadas de antigüedad relacionados con la codificación de información secreta. Según la fuente, si se confirmaran esos avances, piratas informáticos y otros actores podrían descifrar más fácilmente comunicaciones secretas del mundo: transacciones bancarias, cables diplomáticos y correos privados. Steven Murdoch, profesor de University College London, recuerda que el objetivo de migrar hacia un cifrado más resistente era algo así como 2032, y que probablemente no se cumpliría. Mi lectura es que este escenario introduce un riesgo sistémico de doble filo. Si la IA ha encontrado un atajo para romper el cifrado, el coste de actualización urgente para bancos, gobiernos y agencias de espionaje sería enorme, con una carrera contrarreloj para reemplazar infraestructura digital crítica. Si, por el contrario, la IA ha demostrado que ese atajo no existe, el alivio llegaría, pero la incertidumbre actual ya castiga la estabilidad: la sola sospecha obliga a presupuestar contingencias y a replantear calendarios de inversión en seguridad.

Pasamos al sudeste asiático. Según Xataka, Taiwán sufre la mayor fuga de capital extranjero de su historia y la inteligencia artificial es la gran sospechosa. Las ventas netas de inversores extranjeros han alcanzado 1,09 billones de dólares taiwaneses, unos 33.100 millones de dólares estadounidenses, en noviembre. Esa cifra ya supera la salida récord de octubre, de 994.000 millones de dólares taiwaneses. El índice Taiex ha caído alrededor de un 21 % desde su máximo histórico del 6 de octubre y baja aproximadamente un 13 % solo en noviembre. Charu Chanana, estratega jefe de inversiones en Saxo Markets, señala que los inversores están mostrando más interés en otras fuentes de beneficios, ingresos y crecimiento, incluidas las bolsas europeas y la india, el mercado de valores en EEUU y los sectores defensivos. Mi lectura es que esto no es necesariamente un rechazo frontal a la IA, sino una recogida de beneficios y una rotación de carteras hacia mercados menos sensibles a la incertidumbre de chips, aranceles y valoraciones. Aun así, el efecto divisa importa: el dólar taiwanés ha perdido alrededor de un 1,5 % frente al dólar estadounidense este mes, y esa presión cambiaria puede encarecer importaciones y condicionar la financiación de nuevas fábricas de semiconductores.

Cambiamos de terreno. Según Fast Company, el Distrito Escolar Unificado de Los Ángeles ha desactivado silenciosamente los resúmenes generados por inteligencia artificial, conocidos como AI Overview, en las búsquedas de Google de los dispositivos entregados por las escuelas. El distrito, con medio millón de estudiantes, no hizo un anuncio formal, y la medida sorprendió a padres y alumnos. Bridie Lee, líder de Schools Beyond Screens LA, cuenta que fue la comidilla del patio de recreo. En septiembre, los dos distritos escolares más grandes del país, en Nueva York y Los Ángeles, anunciaron moratorias de un año al uso estudiantil de IA generativa. Chris Phillips, vicepresidente de educación de Google, ha dicho que la búsqueda y la IA están profundamente integradas. Mi lectura es que este choque tiene consecuencias económicas para Google más allá del aula. Su dominio de la tecnología educativa estadounidense se apoya en Chromebooks y herramientas como Classroom. Si más distritos empiezan a considerar otros proveedores de búsqueda y Jack Kelanic, director de sistemas de información del distrito angelino, dice que pueden cambiar el motor de búsqueda predeterminado literalmente de la noche a la mañana, el riesgo no es solo reputacional: es pérdida de un canal de adopción temprana y de futura lealtad de usuarios.

Seguimos con las compras navideñas. Según Bloomberg Technology, Google, Amazon, Meta y OpenAI compiten por ayudarte a elegir los regalos de Navidad, y los bots de compras con IA amenazan el dominio de Amazon y Google. La gran pregunta es a quién escucharán los compradores. Mi lectura es que aquí se juega la puerta de entrada del comercio electrónico. Si los asistentes de IA se convierten en el primer filtro antes de comprar, las marcas que hoy dominan la búsqueda de productos y la distribución podrían perder la posición preferente ante intermediarios conversacionales que respondan con una única recomendación.

Terminamos con un choque legal. Según Bloomberg Technology, la pelea por secretos comerciales entre OpenAI y Apple se está ampliando. La empresa de inteligencia artificial acusa al fabricante del iPhone de presionar a proveedores para que rechacen sus dispositivos y de usar acuerdos laborales injustos para impedir que el talento cambie de empresa. Mi lectura es que, más allá del litigio, esto revela una guerra por la cadena de suministro y por el capital humano especializado. Si Apple limita el acceso a componentes o usa contratos para frenar la movilidad, el ecosistema de hardware de IA podría estrecharse, con más costes legales y menos competencia para OpenAI en dispositivos.

Qué mirar mañana: conviene seguir cualquier comunicado de laboratorios de IA sobre criptografía, porque un solo anuncio podría mover a bancos y gobiernos; también los flujos de capital en Taiwán para ver si noviembre consolida la racha de salidas; y, en el frente escolar, si otros distritos siguen los pasos de Los Ángeles y presionan a Google por una separación real entre búsqueda e inteligencia artificial.

stories.title: AI labs sitting on ‘bombshell’ revelations that could cause global chaos, experts warn
stories.summary:
Exclusive: AI may have cracked decades-old maths problems that underpin encryption at banks and government agencies

AI companies are sitting on “bombshell” revelations that could disrupt a cornerstone of security for banks and governments in as soon as a few months, leading experts believe.

Scott Aaronson, a pre-eminent theoretical computer scientist, told the Guardian there were “well-attested rumours” that powerful artificial intelligence models had broken ground on decades-old maths problems related to how the world encodes secret information.

Continue reading...
stories.body:
AI companies are sitting on “bombshell” revelations that could disrupt a cornerstone of security for banks and governments in as soon as a few months, leading experts believe.
Scott Aaronson, a pre-eminent theoretical computer scientist, told the Guardian there were “well-attested rumours” that powerful artificial intelligence models had broken ground on decades-old maths problems related to how the world encodes secret information.
Depending on what has been discovered, it is possible that hackers – and many other people – could in short order have the power to more easily decrypt the world’s secret communications: banking transactions, diplomatic cables and private emails, for example.
If this happened, then spy agencies, governments, banks and private companies could be forced to very suddenly update the foundations of how they communicate, or risk extremely sensitive information being widely exposed.
Aaronson’s and others’ concerns come from a series of mathematical advances that frontier AI companies have announced in the past weeks.
Most of these are abstract breakthroughs. But to experts in the field, they indicate that AI is powerful enough to crack problems that most of them thought would be unsolved for the foreseeable future.
Earlier this week, Aaronson wrote that he was “virtually certain, from multiple reliable sources, that the AI labs are now sitting on one or more bombshells [in cryptography]”.
“The people who thought AI couldn’t do any interesting maths are definitely wrong at this stage, and so it’s no longer clear where the limit is,” said Steven Murdoch, a professor of computer science at University College London.
Speaking to BBC Radio 4’s Today programme on Friday, the mathematician Marcus du Sautoy said “we don’t know” what the broader ramifications of many of these discoveries were, and what this meant for encryption.
But, he added, “no one has been talking about the problem which is at the heart of protecting all our electronic secrets. Why is nobody talking about that problem? Some of us are thinking: maybe they’ve already solved it, and of course, it would have such massive implications that everyone has just kept it quiet.”
Governments, banks and spy agencies have been preparing for the possibility of powerful decryption for the past few years. This is because quantum computers, when developed, will be able to break the decades-old algorithms that underpin many forms of encryption.
But the timeline for quantum computers to be able to do this is still years away, not weeks or months. Murdoch said many governments and technology companies were working towards a higher standard of encryption – one that would not be vulnerable to quantum computers – but slowly. “The target was something like 2032, and that was probably going to be missed.”
Now he, Aaronson and others think there may be sudden advances in what the world understands about cryptography, and these could come soon.
What these revelations could be is less certain. What Aaronson and others think could have happened is that either AI has come up with a new way to break encryption or, conversely, it has proved that such a shortcut does not exist.
This would come from AI models picking apart the maths that underlies encryption, and that up until this point has not been fully understood. If AI has done this, it could find a way to decrypt, and therefore expose, massive amounts of secret data.
It could also prove this information is more secure than previously thought.
The world uses multiple forms of encryption – based on different underlying algorithms – and there are different guesses as to what may have been found, and therefore what systems could be affected.
No concrete announcements have come from AI companies regarding revelations about encryption, said Aaronson, but “anyone informed is assuming” that they are there.

stories.title: Taiwán sufre la mayor fuga de capital extranjero de su historia y la IA es la gran sospechosa
stories.summary:
Algo pasa en la bolsa de Taiwán, porque los inversores extranjeros están retirando dinero de su mercado bursátil de forma masiva. Tal y como comparten desde Bloomberg, la causa apunta a la misma preocupación por la IA que ha estado sacudiendo los mercados en otras regiones. Según comparte el medio, las ventas netas de inversores extranjeros han alcanzado los 1,09 billones de dólares taiwaneses (unos 33.100 millones de dólares estadounidenses) en noviembre. Y eso ya supera la salida récord de octubre, de 994.000 millones de dólares taiwaneses.

Por qué importa. Taiwán es una de las formas más directas para que los inversores globales apuesten por el auge de la IA, porque sus empresas fabrican gran parte del hardware que hay detrás de ella. Así que cuando el dinero sale de Taiwán a esta escala, indica que los inversores están replanteándose cuánto quieren mantener en activos vinculados a la IA. El índice Taiex ha caído alrededor de un 21 % desde su máximo histórico del 6 de octubre y baja aproximadamente un 13 % solo en noviembre.

En Xataka
Huawei acelera su plan para diseñar chips sin depender de Occidente mientras Nvidia limita envíos en Asia

En detalle. Entre las posibles causas, Bloomberg señala las dudas persistentes sobre si las valoraciones de las empresas de IA son demasiado altas, posiciones saturadas en valores tecnológicos, restricciones más estrictas de EEUU a las exportaciones de chips (recordemos que esta semana conocíamos que Nvidia iba a paralizar la venta de sus chips al sudeste asiático), e incertidumbre general sobre los aranceles.

Reequilibrio. Charu Chanana, estratega jefe de inversiones en Saxo Markets, contaba a Bloomberg que los inversores están mostrando más interés en otras fuentes de beneficios, ingresos y crecimiento, incluidas las bolsas europeas y la india, el mercado de valores en EEUU y los sectores defensivos. Así que más que un rechazo hacia la IA, los tiros parecen ir más hacia repartir los huevos en mercados menos sensibles a la incertidumbre de la IA. Chanana también señala que la recogida de beneficios de fin de año se está sumando a estas ventas.

El efecto divisa. El éxodo también está golpeando al dólar taiwanés, pues cuando los fondos extranjeros venden acciones y convierten lo obtenido en otras divisas para llevarse el dinero a casa, presionan a la baja la moneda local. Y es que el dólar taiwanés ha perdido alrededor de un 1,5 % frente al dólar estadounidense este mes, según comparten desde Bloomberg.

stories.title: ‘It was the talk of the playground’: Google’s AI features blocked by L.A. school officials
stories.summary:
School districts are taking steps to block Google’s artificial intelligence features and are considering dropping Google products entirely unless the company gives them a permanent AI workaround, pitting them against the tech giant whose Chromebook computers and learning tools are deeply embedded in America’s classrooms.

In a major step, Los Angeles school officials have quietly disabled AI-generated summaries, known as AI Overview, in Google searches on school-issued devices. The move makes the Los Angeles Unified School District (LAUSD) the largest district to sideline the company, which has said it will not separate its search product from AI tools for education.

The L.A. district, which enrolls half a million students, has made no formal announcement, and the move caught parents and students by surprise, said Bridie Lee, a leader of Schools Beyond Screens LA, which has pushed for screen-time limits and tech oversight in the district.

The group had several members who weighed in at a meeting of the Los Angeles school board’s AI committee on Friday, November 13. By that Monday, AI Overview was gone.

“It was the talk of the playground,” Lee said.

Google is the dominant provider of education technology for America’s classrooms. Beyond its low-cost Chromebooks, the most widely used student laptops, Google’s suite of education apps like Google Docs and Classroom has become integral to classwork, homework, and communication among students and teachers.

But concerns about AI’s impact on learning have ignited a battle between schools and Google. In September, the country’s two largest school districts—in New York and L.A.—announced one-year moratoriums on student use of generative AI, and Google has said it’s not possible to take AI out of its search products. Schools are considering other internet search providers.

LAUSD said in a statement it temporarily suspended AI Overview to ensure student experiences are “age-appropriate and safe.” It also said it continually evaluates its digital safeguards, including third-party tools. It was likely using such a tool that it was able to disable AI Overview.

Schools Beyond Screens LA asked parents to send videos of what laptop screens looked like and received clips showing that AI Overview was no longer an option in Google search on district devices. Then activists reached out to the district, which confirmed AI Overview was disabled. Lee said they had no other details on how it was done or how long it is intended to stay disabled.

“We’re thrilled LAUSD did this,” said Lee. “AI is seeping into everything. It’s dangerous. It’s hurting learning. And it’s a corporate overreach into public schools. It’s Big Tech attempting to strongarm tech policy without anyone’s consent.”

Other districts, such as Fairfax County Public Schools in Virginia, have developed plug-ins to remove AI summaries for students searching on Google, according to multiple published reports.

Google is increasingly at center of school tech backlash

Schools are seeing growing backlash against technology, starting with cell phones and screen time and now focusing on AI, amid concerns that students are using AI to think for them.

The Mountain View, California-based company in August found itself at the center of controversy. That’s when it said it had turned on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students using Google Classroom, its learning management system. Weeks later, New York City and L.A. schools banned generative AI. In New York, the ban applies to all elementary and middle school students, and in Los Angeles all students K-12 are banned from using AI on school devices. Both districts said the ban would allow officials to develop AI policies this academic year.

Then, in early November, Google backtracked. It published a blog post saying it would instead turn off Gemini and all search tools by default for K-12 schools in the coming months. Administrators would have to turn on each tool if they wanted students to access them.

Google said this was to give schools more choice. But the choice to turn off AI altogether is not there.

While the blog post does not explicitly say search can’t be used without AI, Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told The New York Times: “Search and AI are deeply integrated.” If schools ban AI, students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”

The integration of AI in search isn’t new. Google introduced AI Overview in 2025, and anyone who uses Google search will get AI answers to many search results. Google insists AI Overview is an integral part of its search product now and cannot be separated.

Earlier this month, hundreds of Google employees signed a petition asking the company’s leadership to allow schools to turn off AI features “without disrupting their ability to use search as a whole.”

“The way the decision has been reported in the press is poor, and makes Google, and our Education and Search products as a result, look like we’re punishing schools for not using AI,” the petition said. “Many students, educators and parents have concerns about AI in the classroom, as is shown by many school districts who have placed moratoriums or bans on such technology. It is our job as Googlers to respect the user, and listen to them when they have concerns about our products.”

Google has made some changes—but not enough, activists say

Google says it hears parents’ and teachers’ concerns about students using AI to “shortcut learning” and that it shares the same goal: helping students learn. But what many parents and teachers want—the ability to bypass AI entirely and allow students to use Google search like it was in, say, 2024—is not something Google offers. This has forced districts across the U.S. to choose between restricting students’ access to AI and maintaining access to the popular search engine.

Instead of offering an AI-free search product for schools, Google announced a pilot “guided learning” tool that walks students “step-by-step through a range of complex problems, instead of just giving quick answers.”

“We are actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure our products support students and teachers,” the company said in a statement.

Currently, Google search offers AI Overview, which contains summarized answers resulting from general searches, and AI Mode, which is a chatbot interaction. Guided learning, which is not yet available, will walk users through steps intended to support critical thinking to get to the answer.

L.A. schools had already disabled Google’s AI Mode at the beginning of the school year on school-issued student devices, said Jack Kelanic, the district’s chief information officer, during a school board committee meeting on artificial intelligence last week. Educators and staff still have access.

“We understand this as a deeper embedding of AI into the education suite,” Kelanic said. He added, to applause, that the district is not bound to Google’s products if officials determine the changes are not in line with the district’s priorities.

“We have choices,” Kelanic said. “We can change the default search engine literally overnight.”

The Associated Press’ education coverage receives financial support from multiple private foundations. AP is solely responsible for all content. Find AP’s standards for working with philanthropies, a list of supporters and funded coverage areas at AP.org.

—Barbara Ortutay, Jocelyn Gecker and Cheyanne Mumphrey, Associated Press

stories.title: OpenAI Says Apple Pressured Suppliers to Shun Its Devices
stories.summary: The trade-secrets fight between OpenAI and Apple Inc. is widening, with the artificial intelligence company accusing the iPhone maker of undermining its supplier relationships and using unfair employment agreements to prevent talent from jumping ship.
